part2.modelAnswer: Well, I'd like to talk about my uncle who really helped me during a difficult period in my life. He's my father's younger brother, and he's quite a successful businessman living in the city. A few years ago, I was going through a really challenging time because I'd just failed my university entrance exam, and I was feeling quite down and unmotivated about everything. I didn't know what my next steps should be, and I was really doubting my abilities. So, my uncle came to visit us, and instead of just sympathizing with me, he sat down and had a long conversation with me about my goals and what I actually wanted to achieve. He shared his own experiences of failure, which was quite eye-opening, and he encouraged me to see it as a learning opportunity rather than a setback. He even offered to help me find a good tutor and supported me financially during my preparation for the next attempt. Thanks to his guidance and encouragement, I eventually passed the exam and got into a university. To be honest, I felt immensely grateful for his support, not just because of the practical help, but because he believed in me when I didn't believe in myself. It really strengthened our relationship, and I learned that sometimes we all need someone to lift us up and remind us of our potential.

part2.modelAnswer: I'm going to tell you about Kyoto, which I visited last year with my family. It's an ancient city in Japan that was once the imperial capital. We spent about a week there during the spring season, and it was absolutely fantastic. During our stay, we visited numerous temples and shrines, and what really struck me was the sheer beauty and tranquility of these places. We spent hours wandering through the famous Fushimi Inari shrine with its thousands of red torii gates, and we also visited some traditional gardens that were simply breathtaking. One of my favourite activities was actually staying in a traditional ryokan, which is a Japanese inn, and experiencing the culture firsthand. We had authentic Japanese meals and even got to wear traditional kimonos. What I found particularly interesting about Kyoto was the way it seamlessly blends ancient tradition with modern life. Despite being a bustling city, it has managed to preserve its cultural heritage beautifully. The architectural style, the gardens, the tea ceremonies we witnessed – all of it gave me a deep appreciation for Japanese aesthetics and philosophy. I think what really captivated me was the sense of peace and mindfulness that the entire place seemed to emanate. It was genuinely one of the most enriching travel experiences I've had.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a fountain pen that my grandfather gave me before he passed away. It's a vintage Mont Blanc pen, quite elegant really, with a dark blue body and gold-plated trim. My grandfather had used this pen for decades, and he decided to pass it on to me when I was completing my university studies. He told me that it brought him luck throughout his career and that he hoped it would do the same for me. I don't use it for everyday writing because I want to preserve it, but I do use it occasionally for important documents or when I'm writing something particularly meaningful. To be perfectly honest, what makes this object so special to me is not just its material value, but the emotional connection it represents. Every time I hold it, I feel connected to my grandfather's wisdom and his belief in my future. He was a journalist, very well-respected, and I think he wanted me to carry on his legacy of expressing myself through writing. After his death, this pen became even more precious because it's one of the few tangible things I have that belonged to him. It reminds me of his values – integrity, precision, and the power of words. I keep it in a special drawer, and sometimes I take it out just to remember him and reflect on the lessons he taught me.

part2.modelAnswer: Right, so I'd like to talk about helping my neighbour, Mrs. Chen, about two years ago. She's an elderly woman in her seventies who lives alone, and her son is usually abroad for work. One winter, she had a bad fall in her house and broke her wrist quite severely. At that time, I was a university student living back with my parents, so I had some flexibility with my schedule. When I heard about her accident, I immediately went to check on her and found that she was in considerable pain and couldn't do basic tasks like cooking or cleaning. So, I made the decision to help her out for about two weeks until she recovered enough to manage on her own. During those two weeks, I'd visit her place every day, sometimes twice a day. I'd prepare meals for her, help her with housework, accompany her to medical appointments, and just keep her company so she wouldn't feel lonely. It wasn't particularly difficult work, but it required patience and genuine care. What I felt during this whole experience was a strong sense of fulfilment and purpose. To be honest, I realized that helping someone in genuine need is deeply rewarding, not in a material sense, but emotionally. It made me appreciate my own good health and my family's support. Mrs. Chen was incredibly grateful, and we developed a much closer bond. This experience definitely shaped my perspective on community responsibility and the importance of looking out for vulnerable people around us.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to tell you about learning photography, which I started about three years ago. Initially, it began as just a casual hobby after I borrowed my friend's camera during a trip, and I was fascinated by how much you could capture through a lens. So I decided to take it more seriously and actually joined a photography course at a local community centre. The learning process was quite gradual, to be honest. In the first few months, I focused on understanding the technical aspects – things like aperture, shutter speed, and ISO settings. Then I moved on to composition principles and lighting techniques. It probably took me around six months of consistent practice before I felt reasonably confident with manual mode on my camera. However, I'm still learning even now, as photography is quite a deep field with always something new to discover. As for why I decided to pursue this skill, well, it started as a way to express my creativity in a different way. I've always enjoyed visual arts, but photography felt more accessible to me than painting or drawing. Over time, it became a therapeutic hobby as well – whenever I'm stressed or overwhelmed with work, I go out with my camera and just explore my surroundings. It's really helped me develop a different perspective on the world, noticing details I might have otherwise missed. Now I occasionally do some freelance work for friends and small events, which is quite rewarding. I think learning this skill has genuinely enriched my life in unexpected ways.

part2.modelAnswer: I'm quite interested in becoming an environmental consultant in the future. Essentially, environmental consultants work with companies and organizations to help them minimize their environmental impact and comply with environmental regulations. What really appeals to me about this career is that it combines my passion for environmental sustainability with practical problem-solving. I find it quite fulfilling to think about making a tangible difference to environmental issues. To be successful in this role, you'd need a strong understanding of environmental science and policy, which is why I'm currently studying environmental science at university. You'd also need excellent communication skills because you're often explaining complex environmental concepts to non-specialists in businesses. Additionally, you need strong project management abilities and attention to detail. To achieve this goal, I'm planning to complete my degree first, and then I'm considering pursuing some professional certifications in environmental auditing. I'm also trying to gain practical experience through internships with environmental organizations. I've already done one internship last summer where I got some exposure to how these organizations operate. My long-term plan is to work with an established consulting firm initially to build my expertise and professional network, and eventually, I'd like to start my own consultancy focused on sustainable business practices. I genuinely believe that combining career ambition with environmental responsibility is the way forward, and I'm committed to making this happen.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about a book called 'Educated' by Tara Westover, which I read last year. It's a memoir about the author's journey from being raised in a survivalist family with no formal education to eventually attending Cambridge University. I actually picked it up quite by chance when a friend recommended it, and I couldn't put it down. The book chronicles her early life in Idaho where her father was a fundamentalist believer, and she was kept isolated from mainstream society. The narrative follows her decision to pursue education despite intense family opposition and the psychological challenges she faced in adapting to mainstream school and university life. What I found absolutely compelling about this book was the raw honesty with which Westover describes her transformation. Reading about her struggle with cognitive dissonance – between her family's beliefs and what she learned in school – was quite profound. She doesn't paint her parents as simple villains; rather, she presents a nuanced picture of family dynamics and ideology. What made me really enjoy this book was that it goes beyond just being a survival story. It's fundamentally about the power of education to transform lives and the courage it takes to challenge deeply ingrained beliefs. Her writing style is quite accessible yet philosophically rich, which I really appreciated. The book also made me reflect on my own privilege in receiving education without obstacles. Since reading it, I've been much more aware of educational inequalities globally. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone interested in personal narratives of transformation and overcoming adversity.

part2.modelAnswer: I recently watched a film called 'Parasite', which is a South Korean film directed by Bong Joon-ho. I saw it at the cinema about a month ago with some friends from university. The film is a brilliant social thriller that tells the story of a poor family that schemes their way into employment with a wealthy family. The narrative is quite complex – the Kim family gradually infiltrates the Park family's household by pretending to be unrelated, highly qualified workers, and the film explores the class tensions and moral ambiguities that arise from this deception. What I found particularly brilliant about this film was the way it seamlessly blends multiple genres – it's partly a black comedy, partly a thriller, and partly a profound social commentary on inequality. The director uses visual storytelling incredibly effectively. For instance, the spatial relationships between the two families' homes are constantly emphasized, and this visual metaphor of class hierarchy is woven throughout the entire film. The cinematography is absolutely stunning as well. I really enjoyed watching it because it made me think critically about class structures and economic inequality in a way that felt both entertaining and thought-provoking. Unlike some films that preach political messages, 'Parasite' lets the audience draw their own conclusions. The performances from all the actors were phenomenal too – there was a genuine sense of chemistry and tension between the characters. To be honest, it's one of those films that stays with you after you've finished watching it, and I've already discussed it extensively with my friends because there's so much to unpack and analyze.

part2.modelAnswer: One of the most important events in my life was when I graduated from secondary school and passed my university entrance examination. This happened about four years ago, and it was a turning point for me in many ways. This event involved not just myself, but my entire family, particularly my parents and teachers who had supported me throughout my schooling. The actual day of the exam results was quite emotional – when I found out that I'd passed and got into my first-choice university, I felt an overwhelming sense of relief and achievement. To provide some context, I come from a family where I was the first generation to have the opportunity to attend university. My parents had worked incredibly hard to provide me with good education, and there were certainly moments during my final year when I doubted whether I could succeed. This achievement was important to me for several reasons. Firstly, it represented the culmination of years of hard work and dedication. Secondly, it opened up opportunities that wouldn't have been available otherwise – university education expanded my horizons and allowed me to pursue my genuine interests. Thirdly, and perhaps most significantly, it validated my parents' investment in my education and their sacrifices. Beyond the personal achievement, this event was a turning point in my life because it represented a transition to adulthood and independence. Moving to university meant leaving home and learning to navigate life on my own. The experience also instilled in me a deeper sense of responsibility and purpose. Since that event, I've become much more aware of how privileged I am and how important it is to make the most of these opportunities. It fundamentally shaped my current goals and aspirations.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to tell you about my hobby, which is urban hiking or exploring the city on foot. I started this habit about three years ago when I moved to a larger city for university and wanted to get to know it better. Initially, I just walked around aimlessly, but gradually I became more deliberate about exploring different neighbourhoods, discovering hidden alleyways, street art, and local cafes. Now I try to do this at least once or twice a week, usually on weekends, though the frequency varies depending on my schedule and the weather. What I really enjoy about this hobby is that it serves multiple purposes simultaneously. On one level, it's a form of physical exercise that keeps me active and healthy. On another level, it's a meditative experience – there's something quite calming about walking through familiar and unfamiliar streets, observing how the city changes with seasons and times of day. It also satisfies my curiosity about urban spaces and local culture. I often discover small cafes, art galleries, or historical sites that I never knew existed. What really makes this hobby special for me is the combination of exploration and personal reflection. During these walks, I often think through problems or ideas that I've been contemplating. It's become a sort of personal ritual that grounds me. Additionally, I enjoy documenting my explorations through photography and sometimes writing short pieces about the places I discover. This hobby has genuinely enriched my relationship with the city I live in, making it feel less like a sprawling anonymous place and more like a collection of interconnected communities and stories. I think it's an accessible hobby that anyone can pursue, regardless of location or resources.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to tell you about someone I really admire – my high school chemistry teacher, Mr. Ahmed. I've known him for three years during my time in secondary school, and he was one of my favourite teachers. He's a chemistry teacher, but more than that, he's an educator who cares deeply about student development beyond just academic achievement. What makes me admire him so much is his approach to teaching. He never just delivered content; instead, he made chemistry feel relevant and exciting. He would bring real-world applications into his lessons, connecting abstract concepts to practical situations that affected our lives. For instance, he once spent an entire lesson explaining the chemistry behind water purification because many students in our class came from areas where clean water access was an issue. What I particularly respect about Mr. Ahmed is his patience and genuine care for struggling students. Rather than dismissing students who didn't grasp concepts quickly, he would spend extra time with them, breaking down complex ideas into simpler components. He was one of those teachers who remembered that behind every student is a unique individual with different learning styles and circumstances. Beyond his teaching ability, I admire his integrity and humility. He was always willing to admit when he didn't know something, and he'd research to find the answer, showing us that learning is a lifelong process. His enthusiasm for his subject was genuinely infectious – he inspired many of us to pursue science-related careers. I admire him because he represents the kind of educator that I believe can make a genuine difference in young people's lives, not just academically but in how we approach problem-solving and curiosity generally.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd really like to visit Iceland at some point in the future. It's a country I've been fascinated by for quite some time, particularly because of its unique natural landscapes and geological features. If I were to visit, I'd obviously want to see the major attractions like Niagara Falls – well actually, the Icelandic equivalent – the waterfalls, geysers, and glaciers. I think I'd spend time exploring both the natural wonders and also the cultural aspects of the country. I'd love to experience the Northern Lights if I go during winter, and I'd also be interested in visiting the Blue Lagoon and exploring Reykjavik's culture and architecture. Ideally, I'd like to go with my close friends or family members. There's something special about sharing travel experiences with people you're close to. As for why I'd like to visit, it's primarily because Iceland represents a perfect combination of raw natural beauty and geographical significance. The country sits on the meeting point of the Atlantic and Arctic oceans, and it has dramatic geological features that showcase the earth's dynamic nature – volcanic landscapes, glacier systems, and geothermal activity. From an environmental perspective, Iceland is also quite progressive in terms of renewable energy use, which aligns with my interests in sustainability. Beyond the physical landscape, I'm curious about Icelandic culture and how people have adapted to living in such an extreme climate. The country has a fascinating history and a unique literature and artistic tradition. What really appeals to me is that visiting Iceland would combine my interests in environmental science, travel, and cultural exploration. I think it would be an incredibly enriching experience that would deepen my understanding of our planet's geography and human adaptation.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to talk about my smartphone, which I'm sure sounds quite ordinary, but it's genuinely become an indispensable tool in my daily life. I use it for numerous purposes throughout the day – communication, information access, productivity, entertainment, and navigation. I'd estimate that I use it at least twenty times a day, if not more, probably interacting with it every few minutes actually. In terms of what I use it for, it's multifaceted. Obviously, I use it for communication through messaging and calls, but beyond that, I rely on it for accessing university resources, reading news, managing my schedule through calendar applications, and even my banking needs. When I'm travelling, I use the navigation features. I also use it for entertainment – watching videos, listening to music, and browsing social media during breaks. Honestly, what makes it so useful to me is the sheer multifunctionality and accessibility it provides. Before smartphones became ubiquitous, people had to carry multiple devices and tools – a camera, a calculator, a dictionary, a map, a music player – but now all of these functions are consolidated into one device. For someone like me who's always on the move between university, home, and various other commitments, this convenience is invaluable. It also serves as a learning tool – whenever I have a question or need to understand something quickly, I can access information instantly. At the same time, I'm aware that this dependence on technology comes with challenges. Sometimes I find myself checking my phone out of habit rather than necessity, which can be distracting. But overall, I genuinely find my smartphone to be an incredibly useful object that's deeply integrated into how I manage my daily activities and stay connected with people I care about.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to describe the tradition of Tet, which is the Vietnamese Lunar New Year celebration that's central to my family's cultural identity. Tet is celebrated once a year, typically in late January or February depending on the lunar calendar, and the celebration usually lasts for about a week, though the most significant days are the first three days of the new lunar year. The celebration involves multiple rituals and activities. Traditionally, families prepare special foods – we make a particular sticky rice cake called bánh chưng. We also clean our houses thoroughly to symbolize getting rid of bad luck and starting fresh. On the eve of Tet, we arrange offerings for our ancestors and pay respects. We gather for special meals, and it's customary to visit relatives and friends. Everyone wears new clothes, and children receive small gifts of money in red envelopes. Who participates really varies – immediate family members always participate actively, but often extended family members come together as well. For me, this tradition is deeply meaningful for several reasons. Firstly, it's a time when the entire extended family makes a conscious effort to be together, which in our modern dispersed society is increasingly rare. Secondly, it connects me to my cultural heritage and my ancestors. When I'm preparing bánh chưng following my grandmother's recipe or paying respects to ancestors, I feel connected to generations before me. Thirdly, the tradition embodies important values – renewal, gratitude, family loyalty, and hope for the future. The Tet celebration represents not just a new calendar year, but a philosophical reset and a reaffirmation of family bonds. Even though I now live away from Vietnam for studies, observing Tet, even in a modified way, reminds me of who I am and where I come from. It's a tradition that grounds me culturally and emotionally.

part2.modelAnswer: One of the most difficult decisions I've had to make was choosing between pursuing my passion for environmental science or accepting a very lucrative job offer from a large multinational company. This happened about two years ago when I was finishing secondary school and needed to decide on my university path and immediate future. The difficulty stemmed from several factors. Firstly, my family's financial situation – my parents had invested significantly in my education, and the high-paying job would have allowed me to contribute to the family immediately and reduce their financial burden. Secondly, I had received genuine interest from a prestigious company that, on paper, was an excellent opportunity with great salary and career prospects. However, I was also passionate about environmental science and believed that my skills could contribute meaningfully to addressing environmental challenges. What made it particularly difficult was that these two options represented fundamentally different values – financial security and family obligation versus personal fulfillment and societal contribution. After considerable reflection and discussion with my parents, I decided to pursue the university degree in environmental science. My reasoning was that I could always pursue financial opportunities later, but this passion for environmental work felt like a now-or-never decision. My parents were surprisingly supportive once they understood how much it meant to me, though I know they had some apprehension about the financial implications. Honestly, my feelings about this decision have been complex. There's been satisfaction in choosing something I'm genuinely passionate about, and my university experience has confirmed that I made the right choice. However, there's also been occasional anxiety about financial security and guilt about not immediately helping my family financially. But I believe that ultimately, making a choice aligned with your values, even when it's risky, tends to lead to greater fulfillment in the long run. This decision taught me that sometimes the brave choice and the financially prudent choice aren't the same thing, and that's okay.

part2.modelAnswer: Right, so I'm going to talk about a trip I took to visit my grandmother in rural Vietnam about three years ago. I was flying from Ho Chi Minh City, and I had to take several connecting buses to reach her village, which was quite far inland. The main challenge was that the roads were absolutely terrible, basically just dirt tracks, and the journey that was supposed to take five hours ended up taking over twelve hours. To make matters worse, the vehicle broke down midway, and we were stranded in the middle of nowhere for several hours. To be honest, it was incredibly frustrating because I was exhausted, and I had no idea how long the breakdown would take. However, I managed to stay relatively calm by chatting with other passengers, drinking water, and just accepting that there was nothing I could do about the situation. I suppose what really helped was shifting my perspective and seeing it as an adventure rather than an ordeal. By the time I reached my grandmother's house, I was absolutely shattered, but the experience taught me a lot about patience and adaptability. It really put things into perspective, and I became much more grateful for the conveniences we often take for granted in the city. I also gained a deeper appreciation for my grandmother's resilience, living in such a remote area.

part2.modelAnswer: Well, I'd have to say my smartphone is probably the piece of technology I use most throughout the day, without a doubt. Honestly, I use it for practically everything—communication, work emails, navigation, entertainment, you name it. I wake up in the morning and check my messages, use it to plan my day through calendar reminders, and it accompanies me basically wherever I go. What I particularly like about it is the convenience it offers, being able to access information instantly and stay connected with friends and family regardless of where I am. The camera quality is impressive as well, so I can capture memories quite easily. More importantly though, without my smartphone, my life would be significantly disrupted. I rely on it for work-related tasks, coordinating with friends, managing my finances through banking apps, and even fitness tracking. Frankly, I can't imagine trying to navigate a city without GPS, or staying in touch with my family abroad without instant messaging and video calls. That said, I do recognize there's a downside to being so reliant on a single device, and I've tried to be more mindful about balancing screen time with other activities. But ultimately, it's become such an integral part of modern life that functioning without it seems almost impossible.

However, I felt increasingly unfulfilled, as though I was just going through the motions without any real sense of purpose or growth. The decision wasn't straightforward, to be honest. I spent several months researching programs, talking to people working in the field, and really evaluating whether I had the commitment to undertake such a significant change. Eventually, I realized that staying in my current job would mean sacrificing my long-term aspirations for short-term security, which wasn't what I wanted for myself. So I took the plunge, saved up some money beforehand, and enrolled in the program. I'm proud of this decision because it required courage and a certain amount of risk-taking, but more importantly, it's already started paying dividends. I'm now in a position to transition into a field I'm genuinely passionate about, and I've rediscovered my enthusiasm for learning. This experience taught me that sometimes the most rewarding path isn't necessarily the easiest one.

It's deeply rooted in our culture and, well, it's generally celebrated by families gathering together. The festival involves all sorts of traditional elements—lantern displays light up the entire city, there's lots of special food like mooncakes and rice cakes, and children carry colorful lanterns around the neighborhood. There are also various cultural performances, dragon dances, and generally a very festive atmosphere throughout the city. What I particularly enjoy about this festival is the strong sense of togetherness and tradition it brings. It's one of those occasions where families make a genuine effort to come together, which is quite rare in our fast-paced modern life. I also appreciate the cultural significance and the way it connects younger generations with our heritage. Additionally, the whole city transforms into something magical, with decorations and lights everywhere, and there's this infectious excitement that's really palpable. The food is another highlight, as my grandmother makes traditional mooncakes from scratch, and sharing them with family and friends creates quite special memories. Ultimately, it's not just about the festivities themselves, but about the values and connections that the festival represents—family, gratitude, and cultural continuity.

part2.modelAnswer: Right, so I'm going to talk about learning to play the guitar, which I started just about two years ago. I'd always been interested in music but never really had the opportunity or perhaps the courage to actually pick it up. I decided to start learning through a combination of online tutorials and private lessons with a local instructor. Honestly, the first few months were quite challenging—my fingers were constantly sore, and I found it difficult to coordinate both hands. I'd say it took me about six months before I could comfortably play some basic songs and, you know, actually sound respectable rather than just making noise. To reach a more intermediate level where I can play more complex pieces took roughly a year of consistent practice. I decided to learn guitar primarily because I wanted to find a creative outlet and something that would allow me to express myself differently than I was used to. Additionally, I've always found music to be incredibly therapeutic, and I wanted to be an active participant rather than just a listener. The learning process has been incredibly rewarding, not just in terms of developing a new skill, but also in terms of the discipline and patience it's taught me. There's something quite satisfying about being able to play a song that initially seemed impossibly difficult, and I've met quite a few interesting people through local jam sessions.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to describe a time I was quite significantly late to an important job interview. I had scheduled the interview for mid-morning at an office across town, and I'd planned my route meticulously to arrive about fifteen minutes early. However, due to unexpected traffic congestion caused by roadworks I wasn't aware of, I ended up arriving about twenty-five minutes late. I remember feeling absolutely panicked as I sat in the taxi, constantly checking the time and realizing there was nothing I could do about it. When I finally arrived at the office, I was flustered and quite anxious about how this lateness might affect the interviewer's first impression of me. I apologized profusely upon arrival and explained the situation honestly. To my relief, the interviewer was quite understanding, though I could sense it had already created a slightly awkward start. The interview itself went relatively well, but I didn't end up getting the position. This experience genuinely affected how I approach time management now. I became much more diligent about planning ahead and, crucially, building in extra buffer time for unexpected delays. It taught me that punctuality isn't just about courtesy—it actually affects how others perceive your reliability and professionalism. Now, I'm typically quite early to appointments, and I make sure to have contingency plans. It's become a bit of a habit, really, and I think it's improved both my professional and personal relationships.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to tell you about a visit to the ancient Temple of Angkor Wat, located in Cambodia. This temple is absolutely massive and is, well, the largest religious monument in the world, originally constructed in the early twelfth century as a Hindu temple before later becoming a Buddhist site. What I found quite fascinating was learning that it was built at the height of the Khmer Empire's power and represents an incredible architectural achievement for its time. The structure itself is extraordinarily intricate, with multiple tiers and countless carvings depicting various scenes from Hindu mythology. The main tower is particularly impressive, rising high above the surrounding complexes, and the entire site is surrounded by what was originally a massive moat. What really captured my imagination was seeing the intricate stone carvings that have survived centuries, many of which are still remarkably detailed despite weathering. I found the sheer scale of the construction quite overwhelming—it's difficult to comprehend how such a complex structure was built without modern machinery or technology. Beyond the architectural marvel itself, I found it interesting because it represents such an important historical and cultural monument, and visiting it gave me a much deeper appreciation for the sophistication of ancient civilizations. The experience of walking through these ancient corridors and imagining the millions of people who've walked through them over the centuries was genuinely humbling and has become one of my most memorable travel experiences.

part2.modelAnswer: Right, I'd like to describe a problem I encountered at work about six months ago. The company's email system was experiencing frequent crashes, and it was significantly affecting productivity, particularly for our sales team who relied heavily on email communication. I first became aware of the issue when multiple colleagues complained about losing important messages and experiencing delays. Rather than simply reporting it to the IT department and hoping they'd resolve it quickly, I decided to take a more proactive approach. I started by documenting the frequency and timing of these crashes, which helped me identify a pattern that suggested it might be related to the server's capacity during peak hours. I then collaborated with the IT department, providing them with my observations and working with them to analyze the system's usage patterns. Together, we implemented several solutions, including optimizing the email server's configuration and implementing a staggered email backup system. We also suggested to management that they upgrade their server capacity during peak business hours. When the problem was finally resolved, I genuinely felt quite proud, both because the issue was fixed and because I'd contributed meaningfully to the solution. The experience taught me the value of taking initiative and combining observation with technical collaboration rather than simply waiting for others to fix problems. It also improved my relationship with the IT department and demonstrated to management that I was capable of thinking beyond my immediate job responsibilities. Solving this problem reinforced my confidence in my ability to tackle complex workplace challenges.

part2.modelAnswer: I'd like to tell you about trail running, which is probably my favorite form of exercise and something I've been doing quite regularly for about three years now. I initially got into it somewhat by accident, actually—I was looking for a way to make running more interesting because I'd found treadmill running rather monotonous and uninspiring. I started exploring the various trails near my city, and I immediately fell in love with the experience. Now I typically go trail running once or twice per week, depending on my work schedule and weather conditions. What I particularly enjoy about trail running is the combination of physical challenge and the connection with nature. Unlike road running, which can feel quite repetitive, trail running keeps your mind constantly engaged because you're navigating uneven terrain, roots, and rocks. There's an element of problem-solving involved as you navigate different routes and adapt to changing conditions. Beyond the physical benefits, I find it quite therapeutic—being in nature, breathing fresh air, and moving away from urban distractions provides excellent stress relief. The trail running community is also quite supportive and welcoming, and I've made numerous friends through local running groups. There's something quite special about pushing yourself physically while surrounded by beautiful natural scenery, and every time I run a new trail, I discover something interesting about my local area. The sport has genuinely improved my fitness, mental health, and overall quality of life, and I can't imagine giving it up.

part2.modelAnswer: I'm going to talk about a particularly hectic period during university when I was juggling several significant commitments simultaneously. This was during my final year, and I had to balance completing my thesis project, working part-time to support myself financially, and preparing for my final examinations. The main reason I was so busy was that I'd underestimated the time required for my thesis, which involved quite complex data analysis and research, and it coincided with the busiest period at my part-time job. During this three-month stretch, I was probably working or studying almost every day, rarely having weekends completely free. It was quite demanding, to be honest, and there were certainly moments when I felt overwhelmed and questioned whether I could manage everything. To cope with this intensity, I had to develop quite strict organizational strategies. I created a detailed schedule allocating specific time blocks to different tasks, and I became quite disciplined about prioritizing what absolutely needed to be done versus what could wait. I also learned to delegate some work responsibilities and communicate my constraints to my employer, who were actually quite understanding. Additionally, I made sure to protect at least some personal time for exercise and sleep, as I realized that completely neglecting self-care would only make me less productive. The experience was challenging, certainly, but ultimately quite rewarding because I successfully managed to complete everything to a reasonable standard while maintaining my health. It taught me valuable lessons about prioritization, time management, and the importance of asking for help when necessary.
